title: Our Planetary System
intro: Meet the solar system as one family of worlds, in three parts. First a tour: the Sun, which holds 99.8% of all the mass, the four small rocky terrestrial planets, the four giant jovian planets with their rings and many moons, and dwarf planets such as Pluto. Then the four big clues the layout gives about how it all formed: orderly motion, two kinds of planets, swarms of asteroids and comets, and a few striking exceptions such as Uranus on its side and our oversized Moon. Last, how we found all this out: measuring the size of the solar system, then flybys, orbiters, landers, probes, sample-return missions and the missions flying today.

learningObjectives.text: Place the Sun, the eight planets, the asteroid belt, the Kuiper belt and the Oort cloud on a map of the solar system, and explain why one picture cannot show true sizes and distances.
Compare terrestrial and jovian planets by size, density, composition, surface, moons and rings.
Compare Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars by their atmospheres, surface conditions and evidence of past activity.
Compare Jupiter and Saturn (gas giants) with Uranus and Neptune (ice giants), including their rings.
Tell asteroids, comets and dwarf planets apart, and say where each is found.
Use the patterns of motion, and the exceptions to them, to reason about how the solar system formed.
Describe how flybys, orbiters, landers and sample-return missions work, and match each to a science goal.
Explain why the Sun holds almost all of the solar system's mass and where its energy is produced.
Describe the Galilean moons, Titan, Triton and Earth's Moon, and explain why our Moon is surprising.
State the three tests for a planet and use them to explain why Pluto is a dwarf planet.

sections.title: Studying the solar system: what it looks like

steps.title: From points of light to worlds
bullets: For most of history the planets were just bright dots drifting across the night sky. Galileo's telescope (early 1600s) was the first tool that let us study the Sun, Moon and planets as **worlds** with surfaces, weather and moons.
There are two ways to study them: one world at a time (mapping the landscape of Mars, or the layers of Jupiter's atmosphere), or side by side, looking for what they share and where they differ.
The side-by-side method is called **comparative planetology**. 'Planetology' is used broadly here: moons, asteroids and comets count as well as planets.
Most of what we now know has arrived only in the last few decades, thanks to big telescopes and space probes. We have always lived in this neighborhood, but we are only now getting to know it.

steps.title: Eight planets, one huge Sun
bullets: The solar system is the **Sun** plus everything its gravity holds: eight **major planets** with their moons, dwarf planets, and huge numbers of asteroids and comets.
The planets are tiny compared with the gaps between them. Seen with your own eyes from beyond Neptune, the Sun would be a small bright dot and the planets mere pinpoints of reflected sunlight.

So overview maps cheat: to make the planets visible at all, they are drawn about 1000 times too big compared with their orbits. In a true 1-to-10-billion scale model the Sun is a large grapefruit and Earth a ball-point tip about 15 m away.

The eight planets move on nearly circular orbits. **Dwarf planets** such as Pluto and Eris are smaller, and some have quite stretched-out orbits. Even Jupiter, the biggest planet, is only about 1/10 of the Sun's width.

img.alt: Two maps side by side: on the left the inner solar system with the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, and on the right the Kuiper belt around the planets' orbits and the vast spherical Oort cloud around everything.

steps.title: Belts and clouds beyond the planets
bullets: The **asteroid belt** is a doughnut of rocky bodies between Mars and Jupiter, about 2 to 3.5 AU from the Sun.
The **Kuiper belt** is a wider doughnut of icy, comet-like bodies beyond Neptune's orbit, about 30 to 50 AU out. Pluto and Eris live there.
The **Oort cloud** is a huge, roughly spherical swarm of comets at the far edge of the solar system, from about 2,000 to 100,000 AU.
1 AU (astronomical unit) is the average Earth-Sun distance, about 150 million km. Neptune, the farthest planet, is 30 AU out.

img.alt: A line running outward from the Sun on a logarithmic scale, marking the planets, the edge of the Sun's wind bubble, Voyager 1, the Oort cloud and the nearest stars, with distances in astronomical units.

steps.title: Why distances need a log scale
bullets: Neptune is 30 AU out, but the Oort cloud reaches about 100,000 AU. To fit both on one line, each tick mark is 10 times farther than the last. This is a **logarithmic scale**.
On such a map all eight planets crowd into the first part of the line, even though the gaps between them are huge in real life. Spacing on a log map is not a measurement of true distance.

Voyager 1, launched in 1977, has left the Sun's wind bubble (the heliosphere) and is in interstellar space. It is still nowhere near the Oort cloud: it needs roughly 300 years just to reach its inner edge.

steps.title: Not a random collection: patterns appear
bullets: Touring the planets quickly reveals that the solar system has order. Every planet travels around the Sun the same way, and all their orbits lie in almost the same flat plane.
The planets also fall into two clear groups: small rocky worlds close together near the Sun, and big gas-rich worlds spread far apart farther out.
In science a pattern like this demands an explanation. The patterns are the clues to how the solar system was born, and the next unit tells that story.
Questions to keep in mind on the tour: Are all planets made of the same materials? Which ones have solid, Earth-like surfaces? How would you sort them into groups?

steps.title: What comparing the planets has taught us
bullets: **Comparative planetology** is like getting to know a person better by meeting their family and friends: we understand Earth better by seeing it among its neighbors.
Payoff 1: the similarities and differences among the planets guided the theory of how the solar system formed, and so how Earth came to exist.
Payoff 2: it reveals the physical processes (volcanoes, greenhouse warming, erosion, impacts) that shaped Earth and other worlds, which helps us understand and look after our own planet.
Payoff 3: the lessons carry over to the many planetary systems now found around other stars, and to where Earth-like planets, and maybe life, could exist.
It also helps you study: focus on the processes that shape planets, not on a pile of separate facts. Good questions are: What makes a planet habitable? Why did life not arise on the others?

boxes.text: Why does a to-scale map look so empty? Space is mostly empty. The planets are tiny compared with the gaps between them, so no single picture can show both true sizes and true distances. Overview diagrams enlarge the planets about 1000 times so you can see them at all.
Going outward from the Sun: rocky planets, asteroid belt, giant planets, Kuiper belt, Oort cloud. Rock near the Sun, ice far away.

A picture with enlarged planets and neat spacing is not to scale, so it cannot be used to compare both sizes and distances. 'Nearly circular orbits in nearly the same plane' describes the eight planets, not every dwarf planet: Eris, for example, has a stretched-out, tilted orbit. Comparative planetology is not limited to planets: it includes moons, asteroids and comets. The belt and cloud distances (2 to 3.5 AU, 30 to 50 AU, 2,000 to 100,000 AU) come from Ch7.1 slides 4 and 5; Cosmic Perspective 7.1 describes the regions without giving these numbers.

sections.title: The Sun: nearly all of the mass

img.alt: A pie chart of the solar system's mass that is almost entirely the yellow Sun slice, with Jupiter and Saturn as thin slivers beside it.

steps.title: The Sun is almost the whole solar system
bullets: The Sun holds more than **99.8%** of the solar system's mass. It is roughly 1000 times as massive as everything else (planets, moons, asteroids, comets) put together.
So if you lumped all the planets into one ball, it would weigh in at only about **1/1000** of the Sun. Picture an elephant next to a house cat.
Jupiter alone has about 1/1000 of the Sun's mass and is about 2.5 times as massive as all the other planets combined, so it dominates what little is left over.
That is why the Sun's gravity rules the whole system: it governs the orbit of every planet.

img.alt: A photograph of the whole Sun dotted with dark sunspots, next to a close-up of a huge streamer of hot gas leaping off the Sun with a tiny Earth added for size.

steps.title: A ball of gas, not a solid surface
bullets: The Sun's radius is 696,000 km, **109 times** Earth's, and its mass is **333,000 times** Earth's.
By mass it is 98% hydrogen and helium (roughly 73% hydrogen and 25% helium) and only 2% everything else.
Its surface looks solid in photos but is a churning sea of hot gas at about 5800 K (about 5500 °C). The Sun is gas all the way through, and both temperature and pressure climb with depth.

**Sunspots** look dark only because they are slightly cooler than the gas around them; each can be big enough to swallow several Earths. Solar storms sometimes hurl streamers of hot gas far above the surface.

steps.title: Fusion in the core powers everything
bullets: The Sun is a **nuclear fusion** power plant, and fusion happens only in the **core**, where temperature and pressure are extreme. The visible surface (photosphere) and the thin layers above it (chromosphere, corona) only let the energy out.
Each second fusion turns about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into about 596 million tonnes of helium. The missing 4 million tonnes becomes energy, as Einstein's E = mc^2 says.

The result is a **luminosity** of about 3.8 x 10^26 W. The Sun loses 4 million tonnes every second, yet it holds so much hydrogen that it has been shining steadily for nearly 5 billion years, with about 5 billion more to come.

steps.title: Why the Sun matters to every planet
bullets: **Gravity**: the Sun's pull sets the orbit of every planet.
**Heat**: sunlight is the main thing that sets the temperatures of planetary surfaces and atmospheres.
**Light**: the Sun makes virtually all the light in the solar system. Planets and moons shine only by reflecting sunlight.
**Solar wind**: a stream of charged particles flows out from the Sun, interacts with planets' magnetic fields and affects their atmospheres (it also pushes comet tails away from the Sun).
Even so, you can understand most of what the planets are like knowing only this much about the Sun. Its inner workings are studied later, as our model of a typical star.

boxes.text: Why does fusion happen only in the core? Fusing hydrogen nuclei needs extreme temperature and pressure. Both rise steadily with depth in the gaseous Sun, and only the core is hot and dense enough.
Planets together = about 1/1000 of the Sun (elephant versus cat). Fusion = core only. The Sun is 99.8% of the mass, but it is gas all the way through.

'Where does nuclear fusion occur in the Sun?' The answer is the core, not the photosphere, chromosphere, corona or convection layer. 'If we combined all the planets, their mass would be about ___ the Sun's mass' is 1/1000 (not double, half, 1/10 or equal). Ch7.1 slide 7 gives 73% hydrogen and 25% helium; Cosmic Perspective 7.1 says 98% hydrogen and helium together. They agree.

sections.title: Tour of the inner planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars

img.alt: Mercury shown as a grey cratered globe with a close-up of a crater field, a table of its size, day length and temperatures, and an inset of yellow patches of water ice near its north pole.

steps.title: Mercury: baked by day, frozen by night
bullets: Mercury (0.39 AU) is the **smallest** planet and the closest to the Sun: 0.38 Earth radii and 0.055 Earth masses. It is a bleak, crater-covered world without active volcanoes, wind, rain or life.
It has virtually no air, so nothing carries heat around and the sky stays black: stand with your back to the Sun and you could see stars in daytime.
The Sun's tides have locked it into an odd spin: it turns exactly 3 times for every 2 trips around the Sun (58.6-day spin, 87.9-day orbit). Each day and each night lasts about 3 Earth months.

So it has the **biggest day-night temperature swing** of any planet: about 425 °C by day (hotter than hot coals) and below -150 °C at night (about 100 K, colder than an Antarctic winter). Water ice even survives in polar craters that never see sunlight.

Its craters look like the Moon's, but lava plains and cliffs hundreds of km long show past geological activity; the cliffs may be wrinkles from the planet shrinking. Its high density means a very large iron core, perhaps because a giant impact blasted away its outer rock.

img.alt: Venus shown as a pale cloud-covered globe beside a radar-style view of its volcanic surface, a table of its size and temperature, and an inset of Venus shining as a bright morning star over the horizon.

steps.title: Venus: Earth's twin in size, a furnace in reality
bullets: Venus (0.72 AU) is **nearly identical to Earth in size** (0.95 Earth radii) and close in mass (0.82). It is the planet most similar to Earth in size and mass.
It turns very slowly and **backward** (one spin every 243 Earth days, opposite to its orbit). That makes each day and night extremely long, and the Sun comes up in the west and goes down in the east.
Thick clouds hide the surface completely. Only radar from spacecraft revealed the mountains, valleys, craters and signs of extensive past volcanism underneath.

Before spacecraft, writers imagined a lush, tropical 'sister planet'. Instead an extreme **greenhouse effect** from its carbon dioxide atmosphere bakes the surface at about 470 °C, day and night, hotter than a pizza oven and hotter than Mercury.
The air presses down as hard as the water nearly 1 km deep in Earth's ocean.
Why it matters: Venus's greenhouse gas is carbon dioxide, the same gas mainly behind global warming on Earth, so studying Venus may help us with problems at home.

img.alt: Earth shown as a blue globe with swirling clouds, a table of its size, day, year and temperature range, and a small picture of Earth beside the much smaller Moon at the correct relative sizes.

steps.title: Earth: the only known oasis of life
bullets: Earth (1.00 AU) is the only planet known to have life, oxygen to breathe, an **ozone** layer that blocks deadly solar ultraviolet light, and abundant liquid water on its surface. Oceans cover nearly three-fourths of it.

Temperatures are pleasant (average about 15 °C, 290 K) because the air holds just enough carbon dioxide and water vapor for a **moderate greenhouse effect**. Compare: too much on Venus, too little on Mars.
Earth is the **densest** planet (5.52 g/cm3) and the largest of the four terrestrial planets.

Our **Moon** is surprisingly large: about 1/4 of Earth's diameter and 1/80 of its mass. It is not the largest moon, but almost all others are far smaller relative to their planets. The leading idea is that a giant impact, when Earth was still very young, produced it.
Life has been present for about 85% of Earth's history, but our species has existed for only the last 0.007% of it.

img.alt: Mars shown as a rusty orange globe beside a picture of the huge volcano Olympus Mons, a table of its size and temperatures, and an elevation map of water-carved channels coloured by height.

steps.title: Mars: a frozen desert that was once wet
bullets: Mars (1.52 AU) beats Mercury and the Moon in size, but measures only about **half Earth's diameter** and has 10% of Earth's mass. Dust made of iron oxide (rust) turns it red. Phobos and Deimos, its two tiny moons, may be asteroids it captured.

It is full of wonders. Its ancient volcanoes (such as **Olympus Mons**) are far taller than Earth's highest mountains, and its canyon (Valles Marineris) wraps almost a fifth of the way around the planet. Its polar caps are water ice plus frozen carbon dioxide ('dry ice').

Mars is frozen now, yet it clearly had warm, wet periods when life might have been possible: we see **dried-up riverbeds**, **minerals that form only in water** and **rock-strewn floodplains**. Large flows of water probably stopped at least 3 billion years ago, though some liquid water may still be hidden underground.

It looks Earth-like, but you would still need a spacesuit: the air pressure is far lower than on top of Mount Everest, it is usually well below freezing, there is only a trace of oxygen, and with no ozone layer the Sun's ultraviolet light would be deadly.
Over a dozen spacecraft have flown by, orbited or touched down on Mars, and within a few decades humans may travel there to search for signs of past life.

steps.title: Comparing the four, and the spacesuit test
bullets: All four have solid, rocky surfaces, rock-and-metal interiors and high densities (3.9 to 5.5 g/cm3), and all four show signs of **volcanic activity** at some point in their past.

But their **atmospheres** are not alike at all: almost none on Mercury, a crushing carbon dioxide blanket on Venus, a moderate one on Earth, a very thin one on Mars. 'Substantial atmosphere' is NOT a trait of every terrestrial planet.
Hottest on average: Venus (greenhouse), even though Mercury is closer to the Sun. Biggest day-night swing: Mercury (no air).

Could you step outside without a spacesuit anywhere but Earth? No. Mercury has no air and wild temperatures, Venus would crush and cook you, the Moon has no air, and Mars has thin, cold, oxygen-poor air with no ozone shield.

boxes.text: Why is Venus so hot when Earth is not? Both are about the same size and made of the same rock, but Venus's thick carbon dioxide blanket traps heat so well that night brings no relief. Earth has the same gas, but only enough for a moderate greenhouse effect. Same ingredients, very different results: the core lesson of comparing planets.

Why does Mercury's density point to a big iron core? A small planet is squeezed only a little by its own gravity, so a density nearly as high as Earth's means it must be made of denser material than Earth on average: lots of iron.

Mercury = extremes (biggest day-night swing, no air). Venus = Earth's size, hottest of all, spins backward. Earth = densest, liquid water, ozone, life, big Moon. Mars = once wet, now cold and thin. Spacesuit needed everywhere except Earth.

'Which planet is most similar in size and mass to Earth?' Venus (not Mars or Mercury). 'Most extreme difference between day and night temperature?' Mercury, not Venus: Venus is equally hot everywhere. 'Which indicates that Mars could once have supported life?' Dried-up riverbeds, floodplains and water-formed minerals, not its volcanoes, polar caps, moons or the number of spacecraft sent there. 'Which world could you visit without a spacesuit?' None except Earth: Mercury, Venus, the Moon and Mars all need one. Day length: Ch7.1 slide 9 gives Venus a 117-day 'length of day' (sunrise to sunrise) and slide 8 gives Mercury 176 days; the rotation periods in Cosmic Perspective Table 7.1 are 243 days (Venus) and 58.6 days (Mercury). Both are right; they measure different things.

sections.title: Tour of the outer planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune

img.alt: Jupiter shown as a banded orange and white globe with the huge Great Red Spot, a table of its size, day length and temperature, and a glowing infrared image of the planet.

steps.title: Jupiter: a whole new idea of 'planet'
bullets: Getting from Mars to Jupiter (5.2 AU) means crossing more than twice the whole Sun-to-Mars distance, through the asteroid belt.

Jupiter is the **largest and most massive** planet: 11.2 Earth radii, 318 Earth masses (more than 300 Earths) and more than 1000 Earths by volume. Its long-lived storm, the **Great Red Spot**, could swallow two or three Earths.
Its composition is mostly **hydrogen and helium**, like the Sun's, and it has **no solid surface**. If you dove in, the growing pressure would crush you well before you got to the core.
It spins fastest of all planets (a day of about 10 hours) and takes 11.9 years to orbit the Sun. Cloud tops are about 125 K (-150 °C).
It has dozens of moons and a thin, faint ring. Four of the moons (the Galilean moons) are large enough that, orbiting the Sun alone, they would be classed as planets or dwarf planets.

img.alt: Saturn shown as a pale yellow globe with its broad rings, a table of its size, day length and temperature, and a hazy orange picture of its largest moon, Titan.

steps.title: Saturn: big, light and ringed
bullets: Saturn orbits at 9.5 AU, nearly twice as far out as Jupiter. It is only a little smaller than Jupiter in diameter (9.4 Earth radii) but has only about **one-third of Jupiter's mass** (95 Earth masses).
The reason is density: at **0.70 g/cm3** Saturn is less dense than water (1.0 g/cm3). Its fast spin (about 10.6 hours) also flattens it, so it is about 10% wider than it is tall.
Like Jupiter it is mostly hydrogen and helium with no solid surface.

Every giant planet has rings, but Saturn's are the only easy ones to see. Saturn also has many moons, and at least two of them are geologically active now: **Enceladus** (ice fountains) and **Titan** (the only moon with a thick atmosphere).

img.alt: Uranus shown as a pale blue-green globe with thin rings circling it almost vertically, a table of its size and day length, and an infrared telescope image showing its bright rings.

steps.title: Uranus: the planet knocked on its side
bullets: Uranus (19.2 AU) is twice as far as Saturn. It is much smaller than Jupiter or Saturn (4.0 Earth radii, 14.5 Earth masses) but much bigger than Earth.
It is made of hydrogen, helium and lots of **hydrogen compounds**: water, ammonia and methane. Methane gas gives it a pale blue-green color. Like the other giants it has no solid surface.
Uranus is **tipped on its side**, and so is everything around it: planet, rings and moon orbits, with an axis tilt of about 98 degrees. A giant collision during its formation may explain this.
That tilt gives it the **most extreme seasons** of any planet. Near a pole you would get continuous daylight for half of its 84-year orbit (42 years), then, after a very slow sunset, a 42-year night.
It has more than two dozen moons and dark, hard-to-see rings. Only one spacecraft, Voyager 2 (1986), has ever visited.

img.alt: Neptune shown as a pale blue globe with faint cloud streaks, a table of its size and day length, and a deep blue processed image of the planet from Voyager 2.

steps.title: Neptune: Uranus's near twin
bullets: The gap from Uranus to Neptune (30.1 AU) is the longest jump of the tour, a reminder of how empty the outer solar system is. Neptune takes 165 years to orbit once.

Neptune is nearly a **twin of Uranus** in size and makeup. It is slightly smaller (3.9 Earth radii) but denser (1.64 g/cm3), so it is slightly **more massive** (17.1 Earth masses). Its axis is not tipped over.
It has rings and many moons. Like Uranus, it has been visited only by Voyager 2 (1989).

Its largest moon, **Triton**, is bigger than Pluto, has geyser-like vents that spew nitrogen gas, and is the only large moon that orbits backward. That backward orbit makes it almost certain Triton once orbited the Sun on its own and was later captured.

boxes.text: Why can a planet 95 times Earth's mass float in water (in principle)? Density is mass divided by volume. Saturn is enormous in volume and made mostly of the lightest elements, hydrogen and helium, so its average density ends up below water's. Big mass does not mean high density.
Why does Uranus look blue-green? Methane gas in its atmosphere absorbs red light, so the sunlight that comes back to us is blue-green.
By size: Jupiter > Saturn > Uranus > Neptune, but Neptune is slightly MORE massive than Uranus. Distances roughly double each step: Jupiter 5, Saturn 10, Uranus 19, then Neptune 30 AU.

'The most massive planet?' Jupiter, not Saturn. 'Which planets have a ring system?' All four jovian planets, so the answer is 'all of the above', not just Saturn. 'Uranus's large axis tilt causes it to...' have extreme seasonal variations (not very short days, very hot, very cold, or one side always facing the Sun). Moon counts: Ch7.1 slide 12 lists about 115 moons for Jupiter and slide 14 about 300 for Saturn, while Cosmic Perspective Table 7.1 (2022 counts) gives 79, 82, 27 and 14. Counts keep rising as small moons are found, so remember only that the jovian planets have many more moons than the terrestrial ones. Tilt: slide 16 quotes Uranus as 82.23 degrees and Table 7.1 as 97.9 degrees, the same tilt measured from opposite directions. Color: Cosmic Perspective calls Neptune 'more strikingly blue' than Uranus; Ch7.1 slide 17 points out that the famous deep-blue Voyager picture was color-enhanced, so the real difference is smaller.

steps.title: Jovian planets have far more moons
bullets: The terrestrial planets have few or none: Mercury 0, Venus 0, Earth 1, Mars 2 tiny ones. Each jovian planet has dozens.
Most of those moons are small chunks, but a few are large worlds with their own geology. Some are even larger than the planet Mercury.

Most large moons circle above their planet's equator, moving the same way the planet spins. This shared pattern is one clue to how the solar system formed. Many small moons follow odd, tilted or backward orbits.
Moons are not dead by default: some have **active volcanoes** (Io), **thick atmospheres** (Titan) or **liquid water** under the ice (probably Europa).

img.alt: Four photographs of Jupiter's biggest moons side by side: yellow-orange Io, pale cracked Europa, grey and brown Ganymede and dark cratered Callisto.

steps.title: Jupiter's four Galilean moons
bullets: Galileo discovered Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto in 1610, which is why they are called the **Galilean moons**. In the picture they run left to right in order of distance from Jupiter.
No world in the solar system has more volcanic activity than **Io**.
Beneath **Europa**'s icy crust there may be an ocean of liquid water, making it one of the most promising places to look for life.

No moon in the solar system is bigger than **Ganymede**; it even beats Mercury. Ganymede and **Callisto** may also hide oceans beneath their ice, and their surfaces still show puzzling features. Callisto's surface is old and heavily cratered.

img.alt: A strip with the Sun at the right and the planets drawn to the same scale, with names of well-known moons listed under each planet: Moon, Phobos and Deimos, Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto, Titan, Enceladus, Triton and others.

steps.title: Other notable moons
bullets: **Titan** (Saturn) is the only moon with a thick atmosphere. At about -180 °C, Titan is much too cold for liquid water, yet the Huygens probe found rivers and lakes there, carved by liquid methane and ethane. **Enceladus** (Saturn) sprays ice fountains from its southern hemisphere.
**Triton** (Neptune) is larger than Pluto, has nitrogen geysers, and is the only large moon that orbits backward, so it was almost certainly captured.
**Charon** (Pluto) is about half of Pluto's width. The two are locked face to face, so Charon hangs in the sky over one side of Pluto and is never seen from the other.
**Phobos and Deimos** (Mars) are two tiny, lumpy moons that may be captured asteroids. Earth's own **Moon** is about 1/4 of Earth's diameter, unusually large for its planet.
A body is a moon because of what it orbits, not its size: Ganymede and Titan are both larger than Mercury but circle a planet, not the Sun.

boxes.text: Why is Io volcanic when our Moon is not? Jupiter's gravity keeps squeezing and stretching Io as it moves along its orbit, which heats its inside enough to power volcanoes. A moon's geology depends on its heating and history, not just on its size.
Galilean moons in order from Jupiter: Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto. 'I Eat Gummy Candy.' Io = volcanoes, Europa = hidden ocean, Ganymede = biggest moon, Callisto = craters.

'Which planet is orbited by Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto?' Jupiter, not Saturn. 'Moons cannot have atmospheres, active volcanoes or liquid water' is false: Titan, Io and Europa. Our Moon is not the largest moon; what is surprising is its size compared with Earth. Ch7.1 slide 13 calls Callisto a geologically dead 'ice ball'; Cosmic Perspective 7.1 adds that Ganymede and Callisto may hide subsurface oceans. The tidal-heating reason for Io comes from later units; you only need the fact that Io is the most volcanic world.

sections.title: Rings of the giant planets

img.alt: An artist's painting of Saturn's rings up close, with countless chunks of blue-white ice of different sizes drifting in a thin sheet above the planet's golden clouds.

steps.title: Rings are swarms of orbiting chunks
bullets: Saturn's rings look like solid sheets from far away, but they are made of **countless small particles** of ice and rock.
Each particle orbits Saturn on its own, like a tiny moon. They range in size from dust grains to chunks as big as a city block.
A ring is not attached to the planet. It is a flat crowd of separate orbits.

img.alt: A long strip view of Saturn's rings from the inner edge outward, showing many thin ring bands separated by dark gaps, with the Colombo Gap, the Maxwell Gap, the C ring and the B ring labelled.

steps.title: Wide but incredibly thin
bullets: The ring system is enormously wide but extremely thin. A sheet of paper as thin compared with its width would have to be about 2.8 km long.
The rings divide into many thin ringlets separated by dark gaps, such as the Colombo and Maxwell gaps. The C ring and the B ring are two of the main bands.
The thinness is why the rings almost vanish when Earth sees them edge-on.

steps.title: Every giant planet has rings
bullets: **All four jovian planets** have rings; only Saturn's are bright enough to see easily. The terrestrial planets have none.

Jupiter's ring is thin and so faint that most photographs miss it. Uranus's rings are like Saturn's but much darker and harder to see (and they share Uranus's sideways tilt). Neptune's rings are dark too.

Voyager 2 helped discover Jupiter's ring and study the others by looking back at them with the Sun behind them. Rings glow when lit from behind, but that view is possible only from beyond the planet's orbit, never from Earth.

boxes.text: Why do the rings look solid? From far away the countless pieces blend into a smooth sheet, just as a beach of fine sand looks like one surface from an airplane.
A ring is a river of tiny moons. Rings = all four jovian planets. Saturn = the bright ones. Terrestrial planets = no rings.

'Which of the following planets has a ring system? Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, or all of the above?' The answer is all of the above. 'Saturn is the only planet with rings' is false. A ring is never a solid disk. The thinness comparison (a 2.8 km sheet of paper) and the ring-structure labels are from Ch7.1 slide 15, not from Cosmic Perspective.

sections.title: Dwarf planets: Pluto, Eris and more

steps.title: Why Pluto is no longer called a planet
bullets: For 75 years Pluto counted as the ninth planet. Then **Eris** was found in 2005, slightly more massive than Pluto, and dozens of other objects turned out to be not much smaller than either.
That forced astronomers to decide what 'planet' means. Pluto and Eris are now **dwarf planets**: too small to count as official planets, but big enough for gravity to have made them round.

In 2006 astronomers agreed on three tests. A **planet** (1) orbits the Sun, (2) has enough mass to pull itself round, and (3) has **cleared its orbital neighborhood** of other sizable bodies. A dwarf planet passes tests 1 and 2, fails test 3, and is not a moon.

The deciding factor was Pluto's **small size and mass**: it is too small to dominate its zone, which it shares with many similar icy bodies. Its distance, its big moon Charon and its ice-and-rock makeup were not what decided it.

img.alt: Pluto as seen by New Horizons, a pale tan and white globe, beside a telescope image labelling Pluto and its moons Charon, Nix, Hydra, P4 and P5.

steps.title: Pluto and its big moon Charon
bullets: Pluto is a small, icy world: radius 1185 km (0.19 Earth radii), mass 0.0022 Earth masses, density 1.9 g/cm3, made of **ices and rock**, with a surface near 44 K (about -230 °C).
Its average distance is 39.5 AU, roughly as far past Neptune as Neptune lies past Uranus, and one orbit takes 248 years. Seen from there, the Sun looks like little more than a bright star.

Pluto lives in the **Kuiper belt**, a vast band of thousands of icy, comet-like objects beyond Neptune. It is like the asteroid belt, but farther out and made of ice-rich bodies instead of rocky ones.
It has five known moons. The largest, **Charon**, is locked with Pluto so the two always show each other the same face: Charon fills the sky over one side of Pluto and is never seen from the other.
The New Horizons spacecraft flew past Pluto in 2015 and sent back the first close-up pictures.

img.alt: A diagram of the planets' orbits with the very stretched-out, tilted orbit of Eris swinging far outside the orbits of Neptune and Pluto, and Eris marked near the bottom.

steps.title: Eris, Ceres and other dwarf planets
bullets: **Eris** (67.7 AU on average, a 557-year orbit) is slightly smaller than Pluto (radius 1168 km) but more massive (0.0028 Earth masses): the **most massive dwarf planet** known.
Eris is still about 20 times less massive than Mercury, and its orbit is far more stretched out and tilted than any planet's.
**Ceres**, the largest asteroid in the asteroid belt, is also a dwarf planet: round, but sharing its zone with thousands of other asteroids. The Dawn spacecraft orbited it from 2015 to 2018.
Other known dwarf planets include Haumea and Makemake, and many more probably wait in the distant outer solar system.
Size alone would not make Pluto a terrestrial planet: even if it were as big as Mercury, it would still be an icy Kuiper belt body, unlike the rocky, metal-rich inner planets.

boxes.text: Why does 'clearing the neighborhood' matter? A true planet's gravity dominates its orbital zone, pulling in or flinging away smaller bodies over time. Pluto shares its zone with many similar Kuiper belt objects, so it dominates nothing. Counting all of them as planets would have made the list very long.
Planet = three yeses: orbits the Sun, is round, has cleared its orbit. Dwarf planet = two yeses and a NO on 'cleared its orbit'. Moon = orbits a planet instead.

'What was important in classifying Pluto as a dwarf planet?' Its small size and mass, not its distance, its moon Charon or its composition. 'In what region is Pluto found?' The Kuiper belt, not the Oort cloud or the asteroid belt. 'Which dwarf planet is most massive?' Eris, not Pluto, although Pluto is slightly wider. Ch7.1 slide 18 says Charon is 'only slightly smaller than Pluto itself'; by width it is about half of Pluto, so treat it as 'unusually large for a moon'. The three planet tests are not written in Cosmic Perspective chapter 7 or on the slides; they are the 2006 International Astronomical Union definition.

sections.title: Four clues to how the solar system formed

steps.title: A family of worlds, not a random collection
bullets: A big goal of studying the whole solar system is to work out **how it formed**. The tour showed many shared traits that would be hard to blame on coincidence.
Rather than memorize a long list, focus on four big **features** that any theory of formation must explain:
(1) **Patterns of motion**: the Sun, planets and large moons orbit and spin in a very organized way. (2) **Two types of planets**: small rocky ones close in, large gas-rich ones far out.

(3) **Asteroids and comets**: vast numbers of small bodies, gathered in particular regions and with patterned orbits and compositions. (4) **Exceptions**: a few striking oddities, such as Earth's large Moon and Uranus on its side.

img.alt: A top view of the solar system: a yellow Sun in the middle and a red planet on a circular orbit, with curved arrows showing that the orbit and the planet's own rotation go the same way.

steps.title: Feature 1: orderly motion
bullets: The orbits of all the planets are **nearly circular**, and they all lie in **nearly the same plane**.
Every planet goes around the Sun in the **same direction**: counterclockwise when seen from far above Earth's North Pole.

Most planets also **rotate** in that same direction, with fairly small axis tilts, and the **Sun rotates** that way too. So the planets orbit in the same direction as the Sun spins, not opposite to it.
Most large moons travel in their planet's **equatorial plane**, moving the same way the planet rotates. (A 'body' here simply means one object: the Sun, a planet or a moon.)

steps.title: What the patterns point to: a spinning disk
bullets: The **nebular hypothesis** (the subject of the next unit) says the solar system formed from a cloud of gas and dust that collapsed under its own gravity. As it shrank it spun faster and flattened into a rotating **disk**, with the young Sun in the middle.
Everything that formed in one spinning, flat disk naturally circles the same way in the same plane: that explains Feature 1.
The disk was hot near the Sun and cold far away, so only rock and metal could stay solid close in, while ices could also freeze farther out. That fits Feature 2 and explains why comets are icy.

We can check the idea elsewhere: telescopes show flattened disks of gas and dust around young stars, planetary systems apparently being born, in many star-forming clouds including the **Orion Nebula**.

steps.title: How a good theory is judged
bullets: A successful theory must explain all four features at once. Explaining only the shared orbital plane, but not why rocky planets are inside and giants outside, is not enough.
It must also make room for the exceptions instead of ignoring them, because the exceptions record special events in the system's history.

Some astronomers suspect an unseen 'planet nine' far beyond Pluto, based on the orbits of distant small bodies. If it exists it would most likely be one of the exceptions, not a third type of planet, but it may not exist at all.
The method: observe first and spot the pattern; then ask which formation process could produce it; then test that process against new observations, including other planetary systems.

boxes.text: Why does a rotating disk give one shared direction and plane? When a cloud collapses, its spin keeps going the same way and speeds up as it shrinks. A spinning cloud flattens into a disk, and everything that forms inside it circles in the direction of the spin, in the plane of the disk.
The four clues: Motion, Two types, Small bodies, Exceptions. Same direction, same plane, same spin: if all the orbits match, think 'born in one rotating disk'.

'Which is NOT a pattern of motion in the solar system?' The false statement is 'The planets orbit the Sun in a direction opposite to the Sun's rotation': they orbit the SAME way the Sun rotates. Also true: most planets rotate the way they orbit, most orbits lie in the same plane, and almost all large moons orbit in their planet's spin direction. 'Have astronomers seen clouds that look like planetary systems forming?' Yes: many, including the Orion Nebula. Orbits are 'fairly circular and in the same plane', not stretched-out ellipses and not tilted in every direction. The nebular hypothesis and the Orion Nebula disks come from Cosmic Perspective chapter 8, not chapter 7.

sections.title: Feature 2: terrestrial and jovian planets

img.alt: Two photo panels: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars on the left, and Saturn, Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune on the right, all labelled, with the right-hand group far larger.

steps.title: Two families of planets
bullets: The four inner planets are so unlike the four outer ones that they form two distinct classes.
The **terrestrial planets** ('Earth-like'): Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. These are fairly small, dense worlds with rocky surfaces and metal-rich cores. They have no rings and few or no moons.

The **jovian planets** ('Jupiter-like'): Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. They are far bigger and less dense, have rings, many moons and **no solid surface**, and consist mostly of hydrogen, helium and hydrogen compounds.
Planetary scientists often add our Moon to the terrestrial group (it is rocky and travels around the Sun with Earth), giving five terrestrial 'worlds'. It is still a moon, not a planet.

steps.title: Side by side: the full comparison
bullets: **Size and mass**: terrestrial smaller, jovian much larger.
**Average density**: terrestrial higher (3.9 to 5.5 g/cm3), jovian lower (0.7 to 1.6 g/cm3). This is the clearest single split: huge does not mean dense.
**Ingredients and surface**: terrestrial = rock and metal with a solid surface; jovian = hydrogen, helium and hydrogen compounds with no solid surface (and thick, deep atmospheres).
**Moons and rings**: terrestrial = few or no moons (0, 0, 1, 2) and no rings; jovian = rings and many moons.
**Location**: terrestrial = close to the Sun and close together, with warmer surfaces; jovian = far from the Sun and far apart, with cold cloud tops.

steps.title: Hydrogen compounds, 'gas giants' and 'ice giants'
bullets: **Hydrogen compounds** are molecules that contain hydrogen, such as water (H2O), ammonia (NH3) and methane (CH4). They are major ingredients of the jovian planets and of comets.
Jupiter and Saturn are mostly hydrogen and helium; Uranus and Neptune hold a much larger share of hydrogen compounds.

Because these substances are gases on Earth, jovian planets are often called **gas giants**. The name is misleading: except in the outer layers, the pressure inside squeezes them into liquid or other dense forms unlike any everyday gas, liquid or solid.

The nickname **ice giants** is sometimes given to Uranus and Neptune, since their main ingredients would freeze into ices at low temperatures. Their insides are so hot, though, that apart from a few ice particles in the clouds none of it is really ice.

steps.title: Sizing up the extremes
bullets: Largest terrestrial planet: **Earth**. Largest jovian planet: **Jupiter**. Smallest planet: Mercury.
Jupiter is about 30 times as wide as Mercury (71,492 km versus 2440 km in radius) but about 6000 times as massive (318 versus 0.055 Earth masses).

Why so lopsided? Volume grows with the cube of width (30 x 30 x 30 = 27,000), so a planet 30 times wider has room for far more material; Jupiter's lower density brings the mass ratio down to about 6000.
On a graph of mass against radius the planets fall into pairs: Mercury and Mars, Venus and Earth, Uranus and Neptune, Jupiter and Saturn.
Always judge by several properties together: Venus is Earth's size but has a hostile surface, and Uranus and Neptune differ from Jupiter and Saturn in makeup.

boxes.text: Why are there two families? Near the young Sun it was hot, so only rock and metal could form solid grains. Farther out ices could freeze too, giving far more solid material to build big planets that could then pull in hydrogen and helium gas. The next unit builds this story.
Terrestrial = Tiny, Tough (solid) and Toasty, with no rings. Jovian = Jumbo, no solid surface, light for its size, with Jewellery (rings) and loads of moons.

'Which is NOT a characteristic of all the terrestrial planets?' The trap option is 'They have substantial atmospheres': Mercury has almost none and Mars a thin one. 'Which is NOT a characteristic of the jovian planets?' The false option is 'higher average densities than the terrestrial planets': jovian planets are LESS dense. Rings belong to all four jovian planets. 'Jovian planets have more moons on average' is true. Cosmic Perspective Table 7.2 has the full side-by-side list; it uses 'gas giant' loosely for all four and explains 'ice giant' in a footnote.

sections.title: Feature 3: asteroids, comets, the Kuiper belt and the Oort cloud

img.alt: Four grey rocky bodies in a row labelled Ceres 939 km, Vesta 525 km, Pallas 512 km and Hygiea 434 km, with Ceres the largest and roundest.

steps.title: Asteroids: rocky leftovers
bullets: **Asteroids** are rocky (and metallic) bodies that circle the Sun as planets do but are far smaller. Most known ones lie in the **asteroid belt**, which sits between Mars and Jupiter, about 2 to 3.5 AU from the Sun; it probably contains about a million objects over 1 km across.
Small bodies are usually not round: the asteroid Eros, for example, is a lumpy potato about 40 km long. Only the biggest are round.
The four largest are Ceres (939 km), Vesta (525 km), Pallas (512 km) and Hygiea (434 km). Ceres, the largest, is round enough to be a dwarf planet.
There are many asteroids, but the belt is mostly empty space. The bodies are separated by great distances, so it is not a crowded ring of planet-sized objects.

steps.title: Comets: icy bodies that rarely visit
bullets: **Comets** orbit the Sun too, and are small as well, but they consist largely of **ices** (water, ammonia and methane ice) mixed with rock and dust.
The bright comets with long tails that sometimes appear in our sky for weeks or months are actually rare. **Most comets never come into the inner solar system**.

When a comet does come near the Sun, heating makes gas and dust escape, forming a fuzzy **coma** around the solid nucleus and a **tail**. The tail points away from the Sun, pushed by sunlight and the solar wind.
Far from the Sun a comet has no coma and no tail: it is a cold, dark lump. So comets out in the Kuiper belt or Oort cloud do not show beautiful tails through telescopes.

img.alt: A top view of the outer solar system with the Sun in the middle and the positions of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune marked, surrounded by many coloured dots for small rocky and icy bodies gathered in rings and clumps.

steps.title: Where the small bodies live: three reservoirs
bullets: Asteroids and comets are not scattered evenly. They gather in three distinct regions: the asteroid belt (rocky), the Kuiper belt (icy) and the Oort cloud (icy).

The **Kuiper belt** ('Kuiper' rhymes with 'piper') is a doughnut-shaped zone past Neptune, roughly 30 to 50 AU from the Sun. It contains at least 100,000 icy bodies over 100 km wide (the biggest known are Pluto and Eris) and about 100 times the asteroid belt's mass.
Far beyond that, from about 2,000 to 100,000 AU, lies the **Oort cloud** ('Oort' rhymes with 'court'), which may contain a **trillion comets**, most only a few km across.
Oort cloud comets have orbits tilted at random to the plane of the planets, so the cloud is roughly **spherical**, not a flat belt. Its comets can fall in from any direction.
Order by distance: asteroid belt (2 to 3.5 AU) < Neptune (30 AU) < Kuiper belt and Pluto (30 to 50 AU) < Oort cloud comet (thousands of AU, the farthest of all).

steps.title: Asteroid or comet? The difference that matters
bullets: The major difference is **composition**: asteroids are rocky or metallic, comets are icy.
A tail is not the test: a comet shows a tail only near the Sun, and spends most of its life without one. Size is not the test either, and neither is density.
Location is a strong clue: asteroids mostly orbit between Mars and Jupiter, comets mostly live in the Kuiper belt and Oort cloud.
On average, asteroids orbit closer to the Sun than comets or jovian planets do.

boxes.text: Why are asteroids rocky and comets icy? Near the young Sun only rock and metal could stay solid, while farther out it was cold enough for ices to freeze too. Where a small body formed, and still lives, decides what it is made of.
Asteroids: rock, between Mars and Jupiter. Comets: ice, Kuiper belt (a flat doughnut) and Oort cloud (a giant ball). A comet's tail always points AWAY from the Sun.

'Asteroids never have tails and comets always have tails' and 'asteroids are smaller than comets' are wrong options: the real difference is rocky versus icy. The Oort cloud is not made of gas, not a belt in the planets' plane, not the cloud the solar system formed from, and not between Mars and Jupiter; it is a roughly spherical region far beyond Pluto's orbit that may hold a trillion comets. A comet in the Oort cloud is farther from the Sun than Neptune, Pluto or an asteroid-belt asteroid. Ch7.1 slide 5 says 'trillions' of comets; Cosmic Perspective says 'a trillion'. The belt distances and the million asteroids are from Ch7.1 slide 4.

sections.title: Feature 4: exceptions to the rules

img.alt: Uranus as a pale blue-green disk with thin rings circling it almost vertically, so the planet seems to lie on its side.

steps.title: Uranus is tipped on its side
bullets: Most planets spin with their axes fairly upright (Earth's tilt is 23.5 degrees). Uranus's axis is tilted about **98 degrees**, so it rolls around the Sun nearly on its side.
Its rings and major moons share the same sideways tilt. A huge collision while it was forming may explain it.
The tilt gives Uranus the most extreme seasons of any planet: each pole has about 42 years of sunlight and then about 42 years of night.
Its tilted AXIS is the oddity. Its ORBIT is normal: it circles the Sun in the same direction and plane as the other planets.

img.alt: Venus as a yellow-brown globe covered with mottled surface markings in a false-colour radar-style view.

steps.title: Venus spins backward
bullets: Most planets spin the same way they orbit. **Venus rotates the opposite way** (clockwise as seen from far above Earth's North Pole), and very slowly: a single turn lasts 243 Earth days.
Venus still orbits the Sun in the same direction and the same plane as every other planet. Only its spin is backward, and it is slow, not fast.
Because Uranus's tilt is more than 90 degrees, Uranus also counts as spinning backward. So the exceptions to 'planets rotate with small tilts in the same direction they orbit' are Venus and Uranus.

img.alt: Earth, a large blue and white globe, beside the much smaller grey Moon drawn at the correct relative sizes.

steps.title: Earth's Moon is surprisingly large
bullets: Mercury and Venus have no moons and Mars has just two tiny ones, but Earth's moon ranks among the **largest moons** in the solar system.
The Moon is about 1/4 of Earth's diameter and 1/80 of its mass. Almost every other moon is a much smaller fraction of its planet.

It is not the largest moon overall (Ganymede is bigger than Mercury); what is surprising is its size **compared with its planet**. It is not surprising for its craters, its distance or its lack of air.
The leading idea is that a giant impact, when Earth was still young, produced the Moon.

steps.title: Other oddities, and why exceptions are clues
bullets: **Triton** is the only large moon that orbits its planet backward (opposite to Neptune's spin), which points to a body that formed elsewhere and was captured.
Most large moons obey the rules, while many small moons travel on far stranger orbits.
An exception does not break the pattern. A good theory must explain the general rules and also leave room for special events such as collisions and captures.

boxes.text: Why do exceptions matter? The rules suggest the planets formed together in one disk, so a body that breaks a rule probably had a special history: a giant collision (Uranus's tilt, the Moon) or a capture (Triton). Exceptions help us work out which special events happened.
Three famous exceptions: Uranus = tipped on its side, Venus = slow backward spin, Earth = oversize Moon. Plus Triton = backward orbit.

'What is unusual about Venus?' It ROTATES in the opposite direction to its orbit. It does not orbit backward, orbit in a different plane, orbit too fast, or rotate fast; it spins very slowly. 'Uranus orbits the Sun opposite to the other planets' is false: only its axis is odd. 'What is surprising about Earth's Moon?' Its size relative to its planet, not its craters, its distance or its lack of atmosphere. The claim that our Moon is similar in size to the other terrestrial planets' moons is false. Ch7.2 slide 6 lists Uranus's backward rotation as an exception; Cosmic Perspective 7.2 describes Uranus as 'nearly on its side' and Venus as rotating backward.

sections.title: How we measured the size of the solar system

steps.title: Relative distances first, real distances later
bullets: By the mid-1600s **Kepler's laws** gave every planet's distance in AU, that is, compared with Earth's distance from the Sun. Nobody yet knew how many kilometers one AU was.
Find the true length of the AU and everything else follows: every planet's real distance, and from each planet's angular size, its real size.
Several 1600s proposals for measuring it were not practical. The idea that finally worked came from Edmond Halley (of Halley's comet) in 1716.

steps.title: Halley's idea: watch Venus cross the Sun
bullets: In a **transit**, a planet passes directly in front of the Sun and shows up as a small black dot crossing the solar disk. Only Mercury and Venus, the planets inside Earth's orbit, can do this as seen from Earth.
Two observers far apart on Earth (one in the north, one in the south, say) watch the planet cross the Sun along slightly different paths. This shift is a **parallax**.
Knowing the distance between the two observers and measuring the parallax angle gives the distance to Venus by simple geometry, and from that the AU.

Venus works better than Mercury because it is closer to Earth, so the two paths are farther apart and easier to measure. The catch: Venus transits are rare, coming in pairs 8 years apart only about every 120 years.

steps.title: From expeditions to radar
bullets: Halley died before the next transits, but expeditions followed his plan in **1761 and 1769**. It was hard: long voyages, and the start of the transit had to be timed very precisely despite blurring optical effects.

By the mid-1800s these data had fixed the AU to about 5% of today's value, **149.6 million km**. The 1874 and 1882 transits could be photographed, but by then parallax measurements of planets against background stars had already given the AU to within 0.2% (by 1877).

Today we use **radar ranging**: bounce radio waves off Venus and time the round trip. Since radio waves travel at the speed of light, the time gives Venus's distance precisely, and combining it with Venus's distance in AU gives the AU in kilometers.
We now know the layout so well that we can steer spacecraft to precise spots on or around distant worlds.

boxes.text: Why does one number unlock the whole solar system? Kepler's laws already fixed every distance as a multiple of the AU. Measure the AU once in kilometers and you can convert all of them, and then turn angular sizes into true sizes.
Kepler = distances in AU (relative). Halley = transit of Venus parallax (first real AU). Radar = today's precise AU (149.6 million km).

Only Mercury and Venus can transit the Sun as seen from Earth, because only they orbit inside Earth's orbit. Kepler's laws alone never gave the AU in kilometers. sections.title: How we explore: telescopes, people and robots

img.alt: The Apollo lunar module standing on the grey Moon with an astronaut next to it.

steps.title: Where our knowledge of other worlds comes from
bullets: **Telescopes**, both on the ground and in space, have taught us much of what we know.
For one world, the Moon, astronauts explored the ground themselves and brought rocks back for laboratory study.
A few pieces of other worlds have reached us on their own as **meteorites**.
But most of the recent revolution in our understanding comes from **robotic spacecraft**, which have now visited every terrestrial and jovian planet plus many moons, asteroids and comets.

steps.title: How a robotic spacecraft works
bullets: Every robotic explorer carries **computers** to run its parts, a **power source** such as solar cells, a **propulsion** system, **scientific instruments** to study its target, and **radios** to talk to Earth.
It runs mostly on preprogrammed instructions, but controllers on Earth can send updated commands.
Most make one-way trips: they never come back, and instead beam their data home by radio, much as TV and radio signals are sent.

steps.title: Four kinds of mission
bullets: A **flyby** passes a world one time and carries on.
An **orbiter** goes into orbit around the world it visits, so it can study it for a long time.
**Landers, rovers and probes** touch down on a surface or dive through an atmosphere. Some landers bring along rovers or other vehicles (a helicopter, for example) to explore more ground.
A **sample return mission** travels there and back: it gathers material and carries it home to Earth for study.
Which type to send depends on the **science goals and the cost** (and, in practice, sometimes on politics).

steps.title: Planning a mission
bullets: Space travel is complex, scientifically and administratively. Someone must propose the mission (what will it accomplish?), plan its milestones, decide who designs and builds which parts, and pay for it (is the science worth the cost?).
Many agencies fly missions: NASA (USA), ESA (Europe), CSA (Canada), ISRO (India), CNSA (China), JAXA (Japan) and Roscosmos (Russia), among others.
Engineers must choose fuel and propulsion, landing and sample-collection equipment, instruments, and backups in case something fails. Crewed missions add life support.

Exploration usually goes in steps: flyby first, then orbiter, then lander or probe. Sending a lander first is risky: without knowing a world's conditions (Venus's crushing heat, what lies under Titan's haze) it could be built wrong or land in the wrong place.

steps.title: Remote sensing and direct measurements
bullets: Cameras and **spectrographs** measure reflected or emitted light from a distance. **Radar** sees through thick clouds, which is why it is so useful at Venus and Titan.
Landers and rovers examine local conditions directly. Probes that fly into an atmosphere measure it on the way down.
A world's gravitational tug on a passing spacecraft reveals its **mass and density**, something telescopes from Earth cannot measure well.
Mission design always balances science goals, communication delay, power, travel time, hazards and cost.

boxes.text: Why use spacecraft when we have telescopes? Spacecraft get close, so their pictures and spectra are far sharper than any telescope's. They can also feel a world's gravity, look back at rings lit from behind, and sample the surface or atmosphere directly.
Flyby: a brief pass. Orbiter: stays and maps. Lander, rover or probe: local, direct evidence. Sample return: a round trip. Every robot: computer, power, propulsion, instruments, radio.

A photograph alone cannot replace composition measurements or direct surface analysis; each method has limits. Cosmic Perspective 7.3 groups landers, rovers and probes into one of its four categories; the Ch7.3 slides add human spaceflight as a separate, most complicated type and list the planning questions (budget, milestones, failure modes).

sections.title: Flybys and orbiters

img.alt: Left: a spacecraft picture of Pioneer 11 against the starry Milky Way. Right: the Voyager 1 spacecraft with its dish antenna and long boom, on a white background.

steps.title: Flybys: the cheap first look
bullets: A **flyby** passes a world once and carries on. Flybys are usually the cheapest missions, because launch cost depends mostly on weight and fuel is a big part of a planetary spacecraft's weight.
In space there is no friction or air drag, so a spacecraft coasts along its path with no fuel at all. It burns fuel only to change from one path (orbit) to another.
A flyby never has to slow down at its target, so it skips the extra fuel that an orbiter or lander needs for braking.
Its big drawback: it studies the target for a **much shorter time** than an orbiter. Pioneer 11 made the first flyby of Saturn; the two Voyagers (launched 1977) are now in interstellar space.

img.alt: A diagram of Voyager 2's path curving past Jupiter in 1979, Saturn in 1981, Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989, over circles marking the planets' orbits.

steps.title: Voyager 2 and the gravitational slingshot
bullets: Some flybys get more for the money by passing several worlds. Voyager 2 flew past Jupiter (1979), Saturn (1981), Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989) and then headed out of the solar system.

At each planet it used a **gravitational slingshot**: the planet's gravity curves the spacecraft's path and speeds it up, taking a tiny share of the planet's orbital energy (much too little for the planet to notice). This saves fuel.
The boost can be big: New Horizons used a Jupiter flyby to gain about 20% in speed, cutting more than 3 years off its trip to Pluto.

Could we repeat Voyager 2's grand tour now? Not soon. Saturn, Uranus and Neptune take 29, 84 and 165 years to orbit, so the lineup that let one spacecraft swing past all four giants will not come back for well over a century.
Voyager 2 is still the only spacecraft ever to visit Uranus and Neptune.

steps.title: What a short flyby can still measure
bullets: Flybys carry small telescopes, cameras and **spectrographs**. Because they pass a world at a distance of only hundreds to thousands of km, their images and spectra are far sharper than those from the biggest telescopes on Earth or in orbit.

They can see things that are impossible from Earth: Voyager 2 helped discover Jupiter's rings and study those of Saturn, Uranus and Neptune by looking back at them with the Sun lighting them from behind. You only get that view once you are past a planet's orbit.
Instruments can also measure local magnetic fields and sample dust between the planets.
The target's gravity pulls on the spacecraft, which tells us the world's **mass and density**. Flybys supply most of our knowledge of the masses and makeup of moons.

img.alt: Three spacecraft pictures labelled Galileo at Jupiter, Cassini above Saturn's rings and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter above the Martian surface.

steps.title: Orbiters: stay and study
bullets: An **orbiter** goes into orbit around a world, so it can study it for far longer than a flyby. It carries cameras, spectrographs and magnetic-field instruments, and sometimes **radar** for precise surface heights and for seeing through the thick clouds of Venus and Titan.
It costs more than a flyby carrying the same instruments, mainly because it needs extra fuel to brake from its interplanetary path into orbit.

Every planet except Uranus and Neptune has had an orbiter, and so have several asteroids and one comet. Examples: Galileo (Jupiter), Juno (orbiting Jupiter since 2016), Cassini (Saturn, 2004 to 2017) and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.
Galileo and Cassini were deliberately sent into Jupiter and Saturn at the end of their missions, so they could never crash into, and contaminate, a moon that might host life.

img.alt: Three spacecraft pictures labelled Galileo at Jupiter, Cassini above Saturn's rings and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter above the Martian surface.
The Juno spacecraft, a dark central body with three long solar-panel wings, shown against a white background.

steps.title: Saving fuel, and choosing between them
bullets: **Aerobraking** cuts an orbiter's fuel bill: recent Mars orbiters carried only enough fuel to enter a long, stretched orbit, then dipped into the thin upper atmosphere at the low point of each pass.
Air drag slowed them a little each time until, after several months, the orbit was small and nearly circular.
Choose a flyby for a tight budget, a quick first look, or one trip past several targets.
Choose an orbiter for years of repeated measurements and full maps of one world.
A new flyby of Mars would add little today: orbiters and landers already study it far more closely.

boxes.text: Why is a flyby cheaper? Launch cost depends mostly on weight, and fuel is a big part of a spacecraft's weight. In space there is no drag, so fuel is needed only to change path. A flyby never has to slow down, so it carries much less fuel.
Flyby = quick look, many targets, cheap. Orbiter = long look, one target, dearer. Slingshot = free speed from a planet's gravity.

'A significant drawback of a flyby compared with an orbiter?' It studies the planet for a much shorter time. It does not reach the planet slower, carry worse instruments or stay farther away. Juno: one teacher table lists it with the flybys, but Cosmic Perspective Table 7.3 shows it has orbited Jupiter since 2016, so it is an orbiter. sections.title: Landers, probes, sample return and humans

img.alt: A close-up self-portrait of the Curiosity rover on the rusty-brown Martian surface, showing its wheels, mast and instrument arm.

steps.title: Probes, landers and rovers: up close, but local
bullets: The most 'up close and personal' studies come from **probes** dropped into atmospheres and **landers** set down on surfaces.

The jovian planets have no solid surface to land on, so only a probe can go there. The Galileo spacecraft released a probe into Jupiter's atmosphere in 1995; for about an hour it recorded temperature, pressure, composition and radiation until heat and pressure destroyed it.

On solid worlds a lander provides close-up views, local weather reports and automated experiments. Landers have reached the Moon, Venus, Mars and Saturn's moon Titan, and spacecraft have also set down on a comet and a few asteroids.

**Rovers** drive to explore wider areas: Curiosity (on Mars since 2012) and Perseverance (2021). Perseverance brought the **Ingenuity** helicopter, the first powered aircraft flown on another world, and a flying drone called Dragonfly is planned for Titan.
Strength: detailed, direct measurements. Limit: a small area only, and the landing must succeed.

img.alt: Four pictures in order: a spacecraft entering Mars's atmosphere, a parachute opening, rockets slowing the craft above the ground, and a sky crane lowering the rover while the rocket stage flies away.

steps.title: Landing softly is the hard part
bullets: Landing large spacecraft safely has inspired some spectacular engineering. Curiosity and Perseverance used NASA's **sky crane** system:
(1) Friction with the martian atmosphere slows the incoming spacecraft. (2) A parachute slows it to about 350 km/h.
(3) Rockets bring it to a halt about 7 m above the ground, and the sky crane lowers the rover on tethers. (4) The tethers are cut and the rocket stage flies off to crash a safe distance away.
Mars's air is thin, so a parachute alone cannot slow the craft enough; rockets must finish the job.

steps.title: Sample return: bring the world to the lab
bullets: Landers and probes can test rocks or air on the spot, but every experiment must be designed in advance and all the equipment must fit inside the spacecraft.
A **sample return mission** gets around this by scooping up material and bringing it home, where laboratories can study it in far more detail and with tests nobody thought of before launch.
So far, samples have been brought back from the Moon and three asteroids. In addition, the **Stardust** mission grabbed comet dust as it flew past a comet and delivered it to Earth in 2006.
A **Mars sample return** is a top goal: Perseverance has been collecting and storing rock samples for a future mission to pick up.
Bringing a sample home adds a launch from the target and a return trip, which makes these missions far more complex than flybys or orbiters.

img.alt: Two photographs of the orange-brown surface of Saturn's moon Titan, with rounded cobbles on a flat plain, next to a photograph of the Huygens probe, a round capsule.

steps.title: Combination missions
bullets: Many missions combine spacecraft types to get both broad and close-up views. Viking 1 and 2 each took an orbiter and a lander to Mars.
**Galileo** at Jupiter was an orbiter that studied the planet and its moons and also carried the atmospheric probe.
**Cassini** made flybys of Venus, Earth and Jupiter on its 7-year trip to Saturn, then orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017.
Cassini carried the **Huygens** probe, which parachuted through Titan's atmosphere and landed on its surface in 2005, photographing a pebble-strewn plain shaped by liquid methane.

steps.title: Humans in space: the hardest mission
bullets: **Human spaceflight** is the most complicated type, because the crew must survive: food, water, medicine and oxygen; protection from extreme heat, cold and radiation; the biological effects of weightlessness; and no easy help if something goes wrong (as with Apollo 13).
People can make on-the-spot decisions that robots cannot, which is why Apollo astronauts brought back such well-chosen Moon rocks.
Humans have set foot on only one other world, the Moon, and not since 1972. Plans exist to return to the Moon and, within decades, perhaps to reach Mars.

boxes.text: Why is landing so hard? A spacecraft arrives at thousands of km/h and must slow to nearly zero in a few minutes, using a thin atmosphere, a parachute and rockets, with no chance to correct a mistake. A flyby never has to do that, and a probe into a gas giant never has to stop at all.
Flyby: one pass. Orbiter: stays. Probe: dives into air. Lander: touches down. Sample return: brings a piece home. Human: all of that, plus keeping people alive.

'Why would a lander be a bad idea at a jovian planet?' Because the jovian planets have no solid surface to land on, not because they are too far away, impossible to slow down at, or have nothing interesting. 'Which worlds have humans visited?' Only the Moon (the last time in 1972). A sample return does not always have to land: Stardust caught comet dust on a flyby. sections.title: Exploration past, present and future

steps.title: What telescopes and spacecraft have achieved
bullets: In just a few decades, telescopes and robotic spacecraft together have revealed the general character of every major planet and moon, and of asteroids and comets.
Telescopes will keep playing a big part, but for detailed study we will keep depending on spacecraft.
Until recently the planets were only dim lights in the sky. Ours is the first generation to map them as worlds, and no later generation will get to do that for the first time.

steps.title: Missions to the Sun and inner planets
bullets: **The Sun**: it is watched by several space observatories, among them the joint NASA-ESA SOHO, Japan's Hinode, and NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory and Parker Solar Probe.
**Mercury**: BepiColombo, a joint European and Japanese mission launched in 2018, is on its way to orbit Mercury.
**Venus**: Japan's Akatsuki orbiter has studied its clouds, and NASA's DAVINCI and VERITAS and Europe's EnVision are being developed.
**The Moon**: many countries and private companies have missions, and NASA's Artemis program aims to send humans back.

**Mars**: the busiest destination, with rovers (Curiosity, Perseverance, China's Zhurong from Tianwen-1) and orbiters from the USA, Europe, China, India and the United Arab Emirates; Japan's MMX plans to bring back a sample of the moon Phobos.

steps.title: Missions to the outer planets and small bodies
bullets: **Jupiter**: Juno has orbited Jupiter since 2016. Europe's JUICE and NASA's Europa Clipper are headed to Jupiter's icy moons, which may hide oceans.
**Saturn**: NASA's Dragonfly is a nuclear-powered flying drone planned to explore Titan in the 2030s.
**Uranus and Neptune**: no spacecraft has returned since Voyager 2 flew past them in 1986 and 1989.
**Small bodies**: in 2022 DART was deliberately smashed into an asteroid, a test of whether we could push a dangerous one off course.

Japan's Hayabusa2 and NASA's OSIRIS-REx brought back samples from the asteroids Ryugu and Bennu. Lucy will tour the **Trojan asteroids**, which share Jupiter's orbit well ahead of and behind the planet, and Psyche is going to a metal-rich asteroid.

steps.title: See the planets for yourself
bullets: These are real objects, and five of them are easy to see with no telescope: **Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn**. They look like bright stars that slowly shift against the constellations.
On any given night some are missing: a planet may be below the horizon, or lost in the Sun's glare when it lies in nearly the same direction as the Sun.

Mercury and Venus stay close to the Sun in our sky, so look for them low in the west after sunset or low in the east before sunrise. Uranus and Neptune are too faint for the naked eye (Uranus is barely visible under perfectly dark skies).

boxes.text: Why keep sending spacecraft when telescopes keep improving? Up close, a spacecraft beats any telescope for detail, and only spacecraft can feel a world's gravity, touch its surface or bring back a sample.
Uranus and Neptune: one visit each (Voyager 2), nothing since. Jupiter: Juno now, icy-moon missions coming. Mars: the busiest place in the solar system for robots.

Mission dates go out of date fast. Cosmic Perspective Table 7.3 is 'as of 2022'; since then OSIRIS-REx returned its Bennu sample (2023), JUICE (2023), Psyche (2023) and Europa Clipper (2024) launched, and Dragonfly's launch slipped to 2028. Learn the mission types and goals, not exact future dates. DART was a test of planetary defense (deflecting an asteroid), not of protecting other planets from contamination.
